:::{#thm-convex-first-order}
#### First-order characterization of convexity

Let $f : \reals^p \to \reals$ have first partial derivatives
that are continuous on $\reals^p$ ([continuity](vector-calculus.qmd#def-continuous-several)).
Then $f$ is [convex](algebra.qmd#def-convex-function) if and only if

$$
f(\vx) \ge f(\vy) + \tp{\paren{\deriv{\vx} f(\vy)}} (\vx - \vy)
\qquad \text{for all } \vx, \vy \in \reals^p:
$$ {#eq-supporting-hyperplane}

every tangent plane (@def-tangent-plane) lies on or under the graph.
If the inequality is strict whenever $\vx \ne \vy$, then $f$ is strictly convex (@def-strictly-convex).

:::

::: proof

**Only if.**
Let $\vx, \vy \in \reals^p$, let $\vecf{d} \eqdef \vx - \vy$,
and let $g(t) \eqdef f(\vy + t \vecf{d})$.
The inner function $t \mapsto \vy + t \vecf{d}$ has derivative $\tp{\vecf{d}}$ ([vector-valued derivative](vector-calculus.qmd#def-vector-valued-derivative)),
so the vector chain rule ([vector chain rule](vector-calculus.qmd#thm-chain-vec)) gives

$$
\ba
g'(0)
&= \tp{\vecf{d}}\,\deriv{\vx} f(\vy)
&& \text{(vector chain rule)}
\\
&= \tp{\paren{\deriv{\vx} f(\vy)}} \vecf{d}.
&& \text{(a } 1 \times 1 \text{ matrix equals its transpose)}
\ea
$$

For $t \in (0, 1]$, $\vy + t \vecf{d} = t \vx + (1 - t) \vy$, so

$$
\ba
g(t) - g(0)
&= f(t \vx + (1 - t) \vy) - f(\vy)
&& \text{(definition of } g \text{)}
\\
&\le t f(\vx) + (1 - t) f(\vy) - f(\vy)
&& \text{(} f \text{ is convex)}
\\
&= t\,(f(\vx) - f(\vy)),
&& \text{(collect terms)}
\ea
$$

and dividing by $t > 0$, $\dfrac{g(t) - g(0)}{t} \le f(\vx) - f(\vy)$.
As $t \to 0$ from the right, the left side tends to $g'(0)$
($g$ is differentiable at $0$, so the one-sided limit equals the two-sided derivative),
and a limit of numbers that are all at most $f(\vx) - f(\vy)$ is at most $f(\vx) - f(\vy)$.
So $\tp{\paren{\deriv{\vx} f(\vy)}} (\vx - \vy) \le f(\vx) - f(\vy)$, which rearranges to @eq-supporting-hyperplane.

**If.**
Let $\vx, \vy \in \reals^p$, $t \in [0, 1]$, $\vecf{z} \eqdef t \vx + (1 - t) \vy$,
and $\vecf{g} \eqdef \deriv{\vx} f(\vecf{z})$.
Applying @eq-supporting-hyperplane at the point $\vecf{z}$, once toward $\vx$ and once toward $\vy$,

$$
f(\vx) \ge f(\vecf{z}) + \tp{\vecf{g}} (\vx - \vecf{z}),
\qquad
f(\vy) \ge f(\vecf{z}) + \tp{\vecf{g}} (\vy - \vecf{z}).
$$

Multiplying the first by $t \ge 0$ and the second by $1 - t \ge 0$ and adding,

$$
\ba
t f(\vx) + (1 - t) f(\vy)
&\ge t \paren{f(\vecf{z}) + \tp{\vecf{g}} (\vx - \vecf{z})} + (1 - t) \paren{f(\vecf{z}) + \tp{\vecf{g}} (\vy - \vecf{z})}
&& \text{(multiply by } t, 1 - t \ge 0 \text{ and add)}
\\
&= (t + (1 - t))\,f(\vecf{z}) + t\,\tp{\vecf{g}} (\vx - \vecf{z}) + (1 - t)\,\tp{\vecf{g}} (\vy - \vecf{z})
&& \text{(distribute } t \text{ and } 1 - t \text{)}
\\
&= f(\vecf{z}) + t\,\tp{\vecf{g}} (\vx - \vecf{z}) + (1 - t)\,\tp{\vecf{g}} (\vy - \vecf{z})
&& \text{(} t + (1 - t) = 1 \text{)}
\\
&= f(\vecf{z}) + \tp{\vecf{g}} \paren{t (\vx - \vecf{z}) + (1 - t) (\vy - \vecf{z})}
&& \text{(factor out } \tp{\vecf{g}} \text{; matrix products distribute)}
\\
&= f(\vecf{z}) + \tp{\vecf{g}} \paren{t \vx + (1 - t) \vy - \vecf{z}}
&& \text{(collect terms)}
\\
&= f(\vecf{z}).
&& \text{(definition of } \vecf{z} \text{)}
\ea
$$

That inequality is the defining inequality of a [convex function](algebra.qmd#def-convex-function).
If @eq-supporting-hyperplane is strict for distinct points, and $\vx \ne \vy$ and $t \in (0, 1)$,
then:

- $\vecf{z}$ differs from both $\vx$ and $\vy$,
  since $\vx - \vecf{z} = (1 - t)(\vx - \vy) \ne \vzero$ and $\vy - \vecf{z} = t (\vy - \vx) \ne \vzero$;
- so both inequalities at $\vecf{z}$ are strict;
- both multipliers $t$ and $1 - t$ are positive, so the first step of the display is strict,
  and $f$ is strictly convex.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-convex-first-order}
#### Tangent lines under a parabola

For $f(x) = x^2$, the right side of @eq-supporting-hyperplane is
$y^2 + 2y (x - y) = 2xy - y^2$, and

$$
f(x) - (2xy - y^2) = x^2 - 2xy + y^2 = (x - y)^2 \ge 0,
$$

with equality only at $x = y$, confirming that $x^2$ is strictly convex.
For $g(x) = -x^2$ the inequality fails:
at $y = 0$ the tangent line is $s = 0$, and $g(1) = -1 < 0$.

:::
